title: Trump Bans CNN, Politico, and MS NOW from White House
summary:
Journalists from CNN, Politico, and MS NOW have been denied access to the White House after President Donald Trump announced he was banning the outlets. Both CNN and Politico said Saturday morning that their reporters were denied entry and had their badges seized.

Trump said Friday he was barring the three major U.S. media outlets from the White House, accusing them of writing "fiction or lies" about his administration. Press freedom advocates called the move unconstitutional.

CNN reporter Betsy Klein said a Secret Service agent told her that her badge had been deactivated. Later on Saturday, Politico said its reporter Cheyenne Haslett was denied entry and had her pass revoked by the Secret Service. An MS NOW producer was still able to scan her badge to get in, though no explanation was given.

All three outlets have spoken out against the decision, accusing Trump of violating their constitutional rights to free speech and freedom of the press. An MS NOW spokesperson said the White House "belongs to the American people and the decisions made inside are funded by our tax dollars." MS NOW said it "intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy."

Politico Editor-in-Chief Jonathan Greenberger said in an internal email that the company stands by its reporters and will "vigorously defend" their First Amendment rights. CNN said, "We have a right under the U.S. Constitution to do our reporting without hindrance or interference from the government and this ban is an illegal assault on this fundamental right."

In his announcement, Trump did not mention specific stories that prompted the move, but later said "it's really just cumulative stories over the last few years." He added that there "may be others to join them," but has not given a directive banning additional outlets.

The Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, which provides legal services to the media, said it expected the ban to be struck down quickly by the courts because it was "flatly unconstitutional." Its president, Bruce Brown, said, "The First Amendment is clear that once the White House invites in some journalists, it can't ban others because it doesn't like their reporting."
why_it_matters: Who gets to walk into the White House and ask questions decides how much the public learns about the people in power, so this fight is about every citizen's access to information — not just three newsrooms. It also tests whether courts, rather than the president, get the final say over press access.

background_read: The First Amendment, part of the U.S. Constitution's Bill of Rights ratified in 1791, says the government 'shall make no law' abridging freedom of speech or of the press. Because the White House is a government building funded by taxpayers, courts have often treated access for reporters as something the president cannot hand out or take away purely to punish coverage. The White House Correspondents' Association, a group of journalists who cover the president, helps decide who gets seats in the briefing room.

This is not the first clash of its kind. In 2018, CNN's Jim Acosta had his White House hard pass revoked after a heated news conference; CNN sued, and a federal judge ordered the pass restored, finding the White House had not followed fair procedures. Other presidents have also tried to freeze out outlets they disliked.

The groups involved have long histories: CNN (launched in 1980 as the first 24-hour cable news channel), Politico (founded in 2007 as a Washington-focused political news outlet), and the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press (a nonprofit founded by journalists in the early 1970s that gives free legal help to news organizations).

perspectives.description: They argue the president can choose whom to invite into his own building, and that press credentials are a privilege, not a right. In their view the banned outlets have produced unfair or inaccurate coverage, and a president is entitled to push back on it.

They say punishing outlets for their reporting takes information away from the public, whose taxes pay for the White House. Courts have repeatedly ruled that the government cannot retaliate against reporters simply because it dislikes what they publish.

Presidents and the press have clashed for decades, from Nixon's enemies list to the 2018 fight over CNN's Jim Acosta, and bans are often challenged and reversed. The key legal question is whether the ban is viewpoint-based, because that is exactly what the First Amendment forbids.

Expect lawsuits and a possible standoff over briefing-room seats, plus the possibility that more outlets are added to the list. The episode is likely to renew debates about who issues White House credentials and how transparent the process should be.
